title: How Do I Feel?
objectives: I can say how I feel with excited, proud, nervous, worried, and calm.
I can tell about a time I felt each way.
I can show a feeling with my face and my body.
rationale: Naming a feeling precisely lets children talk about big moments at school and at home, such as a first day, a performance, or a loud storm. Excited and proud are good feelings, nervous and worried are tight or fluttery ones, and calm sits opposite the others so children can sort feelings by how they feel in the body. The unit revisits share and together because children can help each other with feelings, and it prepares the story-language units later in the year.

words.def: Very happy about something that will happen.
words.ex: I am excited about my birthday party.
words.ex2: The class gets excited when the bus reaches the zoo.
words.nonExample: A child yawning in bed is not excited.

apps.academic: Tell how you feel: excited, proud, nervous, worried, or calm.
apps.writing: Draw your face when you are excited.

cloze.s: The kids jumped up and down because they were ___ about the trip.

cloze2.s: Her eyes got big, and she was ___ to open the gift.

misuse.s: He was excited about the trip, so he yawned and put his head down.
misuse.why: Excited means very happy and full of energy; yawning and resting show a sleepy child.

visual.alt: A smiling face with star eyes and a party popper.

words.def: Feeling very good about something you did.
words.ex: I am proud of my tall block tower.
words.ex2: Dad was proud when I tied my shoes.
words.nonExample: Feeling sorry about a mess is not feeling proud.

apps.academic: Show a piece of work you are proud of.
apps.writing: Draw something you are proud of.

cloze.s: She worked hard on her puzzle, and now she feels ___ of it.

cloze2.s: The team felt ___ after they cleaned the whole room.

misuse.s: She felt proud of her picture, so she crumpled it and said it was terrible.
misuse.why: Proud means feeling good about what you did; she does not feel good about it.

visual.alt: A smiling child wearing a medal.

words.def: Feeling a little scared about something new.
words.ex: I feel nervous on my first day.
words.ex2: Max was nervous before he sang on the stage.
words.nonExample: A child who runs happily into the room is not nervous.

apps.academic: It is okay to feel nervous when something is new.
apps.writing: Draw something that makes you nervous.

cloze.s: My tummy felt fluttery because I was ___ about meeting my new teacher.

cloze2.s: He took a deep breath, ___ before he spoke in front of the class.

misuse.s: He felt nervous, so he smiled big and ran in with no worries.
misuse.why: Nervous means a little scared; running in with no worries is not nervous.

visual.alt: A face with a tight smile and a butterfly for a fluttery tummy.

words.ex: Mom looked worried when it got dark.
words.ex2: I am worried about my lost mitten.
words.nonExample: A child laughing and playing with no cares is not worried.
words.rel: thinking about what could go wrong

apps.academic: Tell a grown-up if you feel worried.

cloze.s: The boy looked ___ when he could not find his mom at the store.

cloze2.s: I felt ___ when the sky turned dark and the thunder boomed.

misuse.s: She was worried about the party, so she danced and clapped with joy.
misuse.why: Worried means thinking something bad might happen; dancing with joy shows a happy feeling.

visual.alt: A frowning face and a storm cloud.

words.def: Quiet and still inside, not upset.
words.ex: The lake is calm, with no waves.
words.ex2: I take a deep breath to feel calm.
words.nonExample: A child who is shouting and stomping is not calm.

apps.academic: Take three slow breaths to get calm.

cloze.s: After the loud storm, the pond was flat and ___.

cloze2.s: I breathed slowly until my body felt ___ again.

misuse.s: He was calm, so he screamed and threw his shoes across the room.
misuse.why: Calm means quiet and not upset; screaming and throwing is the opposite.

visual.alt: A peaceful face and a gentle wave.

passage.title: Lila on the Stage
paras: Lila waits by the big stage at school. She feels nervous, and her friend Omar looks worried about her.
Lila takes a deep breath and feels calm inside. Then she sings her song to the whole class.
Everyone claps and cheers. Lila feels proud and excited!

qs.q: Lila feels nervous. How does she feel?
qs.why: Nervous means a little scared; Lila waits by the stage before she sings.
Her friend Omar looks worried about her.

qs.q: How does Lila feel at the end?
qs.why: Everyone claps, and the story says she feels proud and excited.

write.prompt: Draw your face and tell a partner about a time you felt proud, excited, nervous, worried, or calm.

study.task: Show each feeling with your face and your body. Which feelings feel big and fast, and which feel slow and quiet?

groups.label: feelings that feel tight or fluttery

sentences: Say a sentence about something that makes you excited.
Say a sentence about a time you felt proud of yourself.
Say a sentence that tells what helps you feel calm.

combine.model: I felt nervous, so I took a deep breath.

discuss: What can friends do together when someone feels worried?
How does your body feel when you are calm?
produce.explain: Tell what you can do to help your body feel calm.

constructed.prompt: Tell about something that makes you excited and something you are proud of.
look: gives a real thing for each feeling
constructed.model: I am excited about the zoo. I am proud that I can tie my shoes.

constructed.prompt: Show with your face and words how someone feels when they are nervous, then calm. Tell what helped.
look: names one thing that helped, such as a deep breath
constructed.model: At first I am nervous. I take deep breaths, and then I feel calm.

teacher.overview: Children learn five feeling words by making faces and body shapes, listen to a short story about a child on stage, and tell about their own moments. The unit stays oral and uses pictures and gestures; no reading is required.

notes.va.excited.adj: Act it out: bounce on toes, wide eyes. Excited is a happy feeling about something coming; children may confuse it with silly. Ask what they are excited about this week.
notes.va.proud.adj: Tie proud to something the child did, not something they own. Ask 'What did you do?' so the word does not mean showing off.
notes.va.nervous.adj: Children often use scared for everything. Nervous is a small, fluttery feeling before something new, such as the first day. Normalize it: grown-ups feel nervous too.
notes.va.worried.adj: Worried is thinking about what might go wrong. Use a calm voice and avoid frightening examples. Teach that a worried child can tell a grown-up.
notes.va.calm.adj: Teach with slow breaths and a quiet body. Pair with a calm-down spot in the room. Calm is a feeling and not the same as sleepy.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'Before the show I feel a fluttery feeling in my tummy. That is nervous. I take a slow breath. Now my body is quiet and still. That is calm. Let's all take a slow breath and say: I feel calm.'
discuss: What does your body do when you feel excited?
How can a friend help when you feel worried?
misconceptions: Nervous and worried mean exactly the same thing.
extend: Make a feelings chart with faces and one child's word for each.
Read a picture book and stop to name how a character feels, using these five words.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit share and together by asking how friends help each other feel calm. Use excited and nervous again in unit 11 when children talk about how story characters feel, and worried in unit 12.

wida.oral: Partner A makes a feeling face without speaking. Partner B names the feeling and says, 'You look ___.' Then they switch.

needsReview: Spanish glosses (emocionado, orgulloso, nervioso, preocupado, tranquilo) have not been reviewed by a native speaker; emocionado can also mean moved or touched in some regions.
Sense boundary: calm is taught only as a feeling adjective (not a calm sea or the noun calm).
Sense boundary: worried is taught as a feeling; the headword is an adjective, and worry as a verb or noun is left to later grades.
